name: Primer tan / base tan
lead: A primer tan or base tan is a tan acquired before a holiday or sun-heavy period. People pursue it for two reasons: for the darker, bronzed skin tone that many regard as more attractive, and in the belief that it will protect the skin from later sunburn so that a holiday tan can be built without burning. It is commonly gained through gradual sun exposure or tanning bed sessions.[1][2][6]

A UVB-induced tan does offer modest protection, roughly an SPF of about 3, meaning tanned skin tolerates up to about three times the exposure of pale skin.[1] The tan itself, however, arises from UV-induced DNA damage.[1] A Canadian survey in 2019 found that the most common reason indoor tanners gave for use was developing a 'protective' base tan (72.1%).[7] Surveys of young people have found that beliefs in 'safe tanning' persist.[3][8]
Public health sources report that indoor tanning raises melanoma risk, and in two US surveys 58% of indoor tanners reported burns during sessions.[2]

paras: Proponents say a base tan prepares skin for intense sun, and that tanning bed sessions give controlled, predictable exposure for building one.[2] Wikipedia lists improving appearance as the most-cited reason for indoor tanning, followed by getting a pre-holiday or base tan and avoiding tan lines.[2] The idea is widely held in the general public, not only in looksmaxxing circles.

UVA (320-400 nm) oxidizes existing melanin, causing a quick darkening that fades and adds little protection, while UVB (280-320 nm) damages DNA and triggers new melanin production, producing a tan after two or three days that can last weeks or months.[1] Dark skin offers some protection but does not prevent photoageing or melanoma.[1] Wikipedia notes that the Fitzpatrick scale, introduced in 1975, groups skin by how it burns and tans, with lighter types burning often and tanning rarely.[1]
The U.S. Surgeon General's call to action, quoted by Wikipedia, states that a UVB-induced tan provides minimal sun protection.[1]

sections.h: History of tanning as a look
paras: According to Wikipedia, before the 1920s tanned skin signalled outdoor labour and lower class. It became fashionable after Coco Chanel returned from the French Riviera with a tan, and Jean Patou launched the first sun tan oil in 1927. In the West a tan came to signal leisure and luxury, while in parts of China darker skin is still often linked to lower classes.[1] Indoor tanning grew from Niels Finsen's 1890 carbon arc lamp, through home sunlamps in the 1920s, to the sunbed invented by Friedrich Wolff in 1975, which reached U.S. sales in 1978.[2]

Indoor tanning is most common among white women aged 16 to 25, according to Wikipedia, and U.S. salon numbers fell from about 25,000 in 2010 to 9,500 in 2016 by industry figures.[2] In the Canadian Community Health Survey, 4.5% of Canadians reported using tanning equipment in 2014 and 3.0% in 2019; among 2019 users, 71.1% were female and 39.2% reported ten or more sessions in the past year.[7][9]

A qualitative study of 21 current indoor tanners in North-West England identified themes including psychological benefits, improving physical health and denial of health risks; participants said they tanned to improve self-esteem and to prevent sun damage by gaining a base tan, and found alternatives did not meet their psychological or physical needs.[6] A survey of 368 New York and New Jersey high-school students found more than 80% viewed movie stars as tan and nearly 60% saw tan people as better looking, while over 90% believed a tan does not prevent further skin damage.[8]

Survey research rather than trials has examined this belief. A survey of 909 21-year-old New Zealanders found that knowledge of melanoma was high but myths about 'safe tanning' persisted.[3] A review in Clinics in Dermatology examined health claims advertised for indoor tanning,[4] and a nursing journal article asked whether a base tan protects or gives a false sense of security.[5] IARC classified tanning devices as carcinogenic to humans in 2009, and a 2014 meta-analysis found a 16% higher melanoma risk among indoor tanners, with a 35% higher risk among those who started before age 25.[2]

Wikipedia reports that overexposure causes sunburn, raises skin cancer risk, accelerates skin ageing and damages DNA. A 2010 study linked frequent tanning-bed use to about triple the melanoma risk, and a meta-analysis estimated indoor tanning is associated with about 450,000 non-melanoma skin cancers and over 10,000 melanomas a year across the US, Europe and Australia.[1][2] Some research suggests UV exposure triggers opioid-related effects, and many frequent tanners may meet addiction criteria.[1]

In 2016 the FTC settled with a tanning bed marketer over claims including that tanning was needed for vitamin D, with refunds of $5.3 million.[2] The US FDA reclassified tanning beds as moderate risk in 2014 and requires a warning against use by under-18s; 15 states and D.C. have banned minors.[2] Brazil banned cosmetic tanning beds in 2009, Australia banned commercial tanning services in 2015, and France was the first EU country to ban under-18s, in a wave of age limits beginning in 1997.[2] Sunless alternatives such as DHA-based self-tanners, bronzers and spray tans give colour without UV exposure.[1]

card.summary: Tanning in advance to avoid burns later; a UV-induced tan gives only modest protection (around SPF 3) and comes from the same DNA damage.
card.note: The tan results from UV damage; indoor tanning is classified as carcinogenic.

quick.overview:
A primer or base tan is a tan built up before sun exposure in the belief that it will prevent later sunburn. It is often gained through gradual sun or tanning beds.

Research describes a UVB-induced tan as giving modest protection, roughly SPF 3.
quick.mechanism: UVB damages skin-cell DNA and triggers melanin production, which absorbs some UV. UVA darkening of existing melanin gives quick colour but adds no real protection.
quick.risks: UV exposure causes sunburn and is linked to skin cancer and ageing. Tanning devices are classified as carcinogenic to humans, and surveys found most indoor tanners had burned during sessions.

chain: Skin darkens to a tan before the main sun period
Bronzed look, and a tan that tolerates more exposure than pale skin
angle.text: A base tan darkens skin ahead of a holiday or event, which is the look people are seeking, and users say it lets them spend time in the sun with less burning. UVB tans give about SPF 3 of protection according to Wikipedia.
